title: Absolution and penance
hookLine: I absolve you, and a small penance to begin the repair

lines: A FEW WORDS, AND A SMALL JOB.
cards: A hiker carries a heavy pack so long she forgets it's there. She just walks a little bent over. Then someone lifts it off her shoulders, and for a second she nearly floats.
Some people who come out of confession after years away describe it like that. They sit in the pew afterward, a bit stunned, lighter.
What happened in there came down to a few words spoken by a priest, and then a small job to do on the way out.

teach.b: Absolution comes from the Latin absolvere, to loosen, to set free, to untie, the same root as absolute and solve. When the priest absolves, Catholics believe the knots are untied.
After the penitent's act of contrition, he extends his hand over their head and prays a short prayer of absolution.

It names God as the Father of mercies, who reconciled the world through the death and resurrection of his Son and sent the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins. It ends with the words at the heart of the sacrament.
In the old Latin form: Ego te absolvo a peccatis tuis, in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti. I absolve you from your sins, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.
The penitent answers amen. Catholics believe every sin confessed with real sorrow is forgiven then and there, completely. Then comes the piece that's often misunderstood: the penance.
The priest gives a small task, often a few prayers, sometimes an act of kindness, reading a passage, or making something right.
It isn't payment. You can't buy forgiveness, and the Church says so. It's more like physical therapy after surgery.
The sin is forgiven, but it has left some damage, in you and around you, and penance begins the repair. When you can, that means real repair: returning what was taken, fixing what was broken.

Zacchaeus, the tax collector, shows it. In the Douay-Rheims, he tells Jesus: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have wronged any man of any thing, I restore him fourfold."
Forgiven, and then sent out to mend.

how: At the end of confession the priest extends his hand and says the words of absolution; the penitent answers amen and later does the penance he gave, often a few prayers or a small act of repair.

o: the priest's words that forgive and untie your sins
a pardon you earn by doing enough penance
a ritual washing before you enter a church

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: a penance is how you pay for forgiveness
forgiveness can't be bought; penance begins repairing the damage sin leaves.
absolution comes from a Latin word for untying
absolvere: to loosen, to set free.
a penance is always a set of prayers
it can be prayers, an act of kindness, a reading, or making something right.

games.q: you're Zacchaeus. Jesus has just come to eat at your house, and the crowd is grumbling about your cheating. what do you do?
o: tell the crowd to mind their own business.
give half to the poor and pay back fourfold anyone you wronged.
quietly promise to do better next time.
games.why: "the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have wronged any man of any thing, I restore him fourfold." forgiveness became repair.

practice: Think back over what you've looked at this week and find something you damaged, even a little: a trust, a friendship, a borrowed thing, a reputation you shaded in conversation.
Choose one small, concrete act that would begin to fix it, a call, a correction, giving something back, something doable. If you pray, ask for help to do it well.

wordCard.voice: Absolution. From the Latin for untying. The priest's words of forgiveness, and after them, a small penance to begin the repair. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: I absolve you. The heart of the words of absolution, from absolvere, to untie.

carryVoice: Your line: forgiven, then sent. The knots are untied first; the repair comes after. Until tomorrow.
